catalog_quote: This chapter discusses aspects of prosody in SuNdaLa, specifically tone and reduplication. ... Tone assignment in nouns is unpredictable and has therefore to be lexically marked.Verbs show purely accentual properties as there is always one high tone in a construction which is assigned in one position (either the penultimate or antepenultimate mora). ... The tone system of verbs in SuNdaLa is fundamentally different from that of nominals.While for nouns the assignment of high tones is not predictable, it is predictable for verbs; thus the tone system of verbs has characteristics of an accentual rather than a pure tone system. ... Like in most other Bantu languages the presence of H tones in SuNdaLa is also determined largely by tense morphemes. sweep_summary: Ndali (ndal1241) is in the catalog as tonal on Mtenje 2016 (UCT PhD, open, held by the project). Of the 21 search titles, 20 are Glottolog keyword misassignments (papers on English, Korean, Chinese, Old English, German, theory) triggered by the word 'prosodically'; only Botne 1998 (SAL 27(1), open, already held by the project) is about Ndali. Read in full: it treats Chindali prominence as high tone '(accent)' with mora-counted vowel shortening, speculates tone is 'becoming more stress-like', and posits no word-stress rule, so it confirms the tonal coding without superseding Mtenje 2016. Hyman 2009 (held by the project) cites Ndali once, silent on stress (its Ndali line is on printed p.205, not p.204 as the 9/16 row says). New this search of works with stress in the title: Botne 2008 Grammatical Sketch of Chindali now has chapter DOIs at degruyterbrill.com (Part 1: Phonology pp.5-16, doi:10.70249/9780871693037-005); access could not be confirmed (HTTP 202 empty body, no Crossref license), high priority to acquire. Mtenje 2006 'Tone in Cindali' (Lingua) is closed (no OA copy, abstract withheld); Kabuje 1995 (UDSM MA) not located; the Botne & Schafer 2008 dictionary is an archive.org lending copy only. all probes and records with.

new_statements.reading: First-hand description of Malawian Chindali by a field linguist: word-level prominence is lexical high tone (which Botne glosses as 'accent'), with vowel length governed by mora count and by the presence of a prefix H; 'penultimate prominence' is invoked only as a diachronic Bantu preference, and no synchronic word-stress rule is stated. This confirms the catalog's tonal-OR-pitch accent coding and adds nothing that would license a stress rule.

sources.locator: p.97 (abstract), p.106 n.5, p.117 (section 11), p.120 (section 13); pp.1, 10, 21, 24
sources.note: The only works with stress in the title genuinely about Ndali. Describes Malawian Chindali noun prosody entirely in terms of high tone and mora count: prefix-vowel shortening is blocked by a high tone on the prefix, which Botne glosses as '(accent)'; he speculates that tone is 'becoming more stress-like' and invokes a diachronic Bantu 'preference for penultimate prominence', but posits no word-stress rule and marks lexical H tones throughout. Confirms the catalog's tonal-OR-pitch accent coding (lexical tone in nouns).
